title: The news, and how far to trust it
cando: follow news stories and judge how reliable they are

about.text: Every day, news reaches us from newspapers, websites, friends and social media, and not all of it is true. In this lesson you discuss a news story, learn how reports and headlines say who is claiming what, and compare one story told by three different outlets. At the end, you present a story yourself and say how far you trust it, and why.
goals: Discuss a news story and say where you heard it: According to…, Apparently…, I read somewhere that…
Understand and use reporting passives: It is said that…, He is thought to be…
Read headlines correctly, and see what they claim and what they do not.
Compare three reports of one story and write a short report that says who claims what.
Present a news story and explain how far you trust it.

chapters.title: Did you see the news?
chapters.text:
This lesson is about the news, and about how far to trust it.
First, you listen to two colleagues, Mei and Carlos. A story about their town has gone viral on social media, and Carlos is worried.
Listen to how they talk about it. They do not just repeat the story. They say where it came from. According to the local paper… Apparently… I read somewhere that…
These phrases are important. They tell the listener how close you are to the facts. Notice that Mei is sceptical. She wants to know the source before she believes anything, and she does not share the story until she knows more.

chapters.title: Who says so?
chapters.text:
Next, the grammar. There are two parts.
Part one is the reporting passive. News reports use it all the time. It is said that the factory will close. The director is thought to be leaving. These sentences report a claim, but they do not say whose claim it is. So always ask: said by whom?
Part two is how headlines work. Headlines use very few words, and they have their own grammar. Factory closes means the factory has closed, or is closing. Jobs cut means jobs have been cut. Minister to resign means the minister is going to resign. Read a headline carefully, and then read the story under it.

chapters.title: One story, three outlets
chapters.text:
Then you read one story, reported by three different outlets: a local newspaper, a news website and a popular gossip site.
The facts are the same, but the stories are not. Look at the headlines. Look at who each report quotes. A named spokesperson? An anonymous source? Nobody at all?
Then look at what each outlet has checked. One says clearly what it could not verify. Another calls its story exclusive, but gives you very little to check.
After that, you write a short report of your own. Say who claims what, and what has not been checked yet.

chapters.title: Presenting a story
chapters.text:
In the live class, you present a news story. It can be from your country, your town or your work. Choose a story you know well.
First, tell the story briefly. Then say where it came from and how much you trust it. Give your reasons. Is the source named? Have other outlets checked it? Does anybody gain from the story?
The other learners will ask you questions, so be ready. You do not need to be sure. It is fine to say: I'd take it with a pinch of salt.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text connected with the news. It may be a story, an article or a chapter of a book.
Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
As you read, ask the questions from this lesson: who is speaking, how do they know, and what might they not be saying?

warmup.prompt: Where do you get most of your news?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Most people use more than one. The question in this lesson is not where news comes from, but how far you can trust it.

conversation.title: Is it true?
conversation.setting: Carlos and Mei work together at a delivery company in Millbrook. At lunch, Carlos shows Mei a story on his phone.
lines: Carlos
Have you seen this? Apparently Norland Foods is closing its Millbrook factory. Three hundred jobs.
Mei
Really? Where did you see that?
Carlos
It's all over social media. It's gone viral since this morning. My cousin works there, and he's really worried.
Mei
I'm not surprised. But is it breaking news, or just a rumour? Who's the source?
Carlos
According to a post I saw, a manager told staff yesterday. It is said that the factory will close before Christmas.
Mei
Said by whom, though? A post on social media isn't exactly trustworthy.
Carlos
True. But I read somewhere that the company is thought to be losing money.
Mei
That might be right. Mind you, a lot of sites make stories sound more sensational than they are. Has anyone fact-checked it?
Carlos
Not that I know of. The coverage so far is all on gossip sites.
Mei
Then I'd take it with a pinch of salt. Remember the scandal about the mayor last year? It spread everywhere, and it turned out to be fake news.
Carlos
You're right. I should probably be more sceptical.
Mei
Let's see what the local paper says. If the company really is planning something, the paper will reveal it soon enough.

questions.q: Where did Carlos see the story?
questions.why: He says: It's all over social media.

questions.a: The source is unclear, and nobody has checked the story.
wrong: She knows the factory is doing well.
questions.why: She asks who the source is and whether anyone has fact-checked it.

questions.q: What do they decide to do?
questions.a: wait and see what the local paper reports
wrong: share the post with their friends
questions.why: Mei says: Let's see what the local paper says.

phrases.use: Passing on something you have heard, without saying it is certain.

phrases.text: According to a post I saw, …
phrases.use: Saying where a piece of news came from.
Passing on news when you cannot remember exactly where it came from.
Asking where a story comes from.
Questioning a claim that names nobody.
Asking whether a story has been checked.

phrases.text: I'd take it with a pinch of salt.
phrases.use: Saying you do not fully believe something.

items.meaning: News about an event that is happening now, or has only just happened.
items.example: The programme stopped for breaking news about a fire at the airport.

items.meaning: False stories made to look like real reports, often to mislead people.
items.example: The photo was fake news: it was taken three years earlier, in another country.

items.meaning: Websites and apps where people share posts, photos and videos with each other.
items.example: Many people now get most of their news from social media.

items.meaning: The person, document or organisation that a piece of information comes from.
items.example: A good journalist checks every source.

items.meaning: A story that people pass on to each other, which may or may not be true.
items.example: There's a rumour that the office is moving.

items.meaning: Something that shocks the public, especially dishonest behaviour by important people.
items.example: The minister resigned after a scandal about his expenses.

items.meaning: The way the news reports an event, and how much it reports it.
items.example: The match got a lot of coverage on television.

items.meaning: To make something known that was secret or hidden.
items.example: The report revealed that the company had ignored the warnings.

items.meaning: To move quickly and reach more and more people.
items.example: The story spread across the town in a few hours.

items.meaning: When a post, photo or video is shared very quickly by huge numbers of people online.
items.example: Her video of the flood went viral overnight.

items.meaning: To find out whether the facts in a statement or a story are true.
items.example: Always fact-check a figure before you put it in a report.

items.meaning: Able to be believed or relied on.
items.example: Is this website trustworthy, or does it just want clicks?

items.meaning: Not easily convinced; having doubts about whether something is true.
items.example: I'm sceptical about stories with no named source.

items.meaning: Written to shock or excite people, rather than to inform them.
items.example: The headline was sensational, but the article said very little.

items.w: take with a pinch of salt
items.meaning: To not completely believe something, because it may be untrue or exaggerated.
items.example: Take his figures with a pinch of salt: he always exaggerates.

sound.title: Headlines out loud
sound.explain: A headline keeps only the important words. When you say the full sentence, the small words come back, but they are quick and weak: has, have been, is going to. The stress stays on the important words. Listen, then say each pair.
groups: Factory closes · the factory has closed
Jobs cut · jobs have been cut
Minister to resign · the minister is going to resign
lines: According to the paper, three hundred jobs have been cut.
The factory is said to be closing.
I'd take it with a pinch of salt.

sayIt.instructions: Say Mei's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound calm and sceptical, not rude?
lines: I'm not surprised. But is it breaking news, or just a rumour? Who's the source?
Said by whom, though? A post on social media isn't exactly trustworthy.
Then I'd take it with a pinch of salt.
Let's see what the local paper says.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Each one reports a piece of news. Look at who is named as the source.
examples: It is said that the factory will close before Christmas.
The company is thought to be losing money.
According to a post I saw, a manager told staff yesterday.
spot.question: Two sentences report a claim without saying who made it. Which two? What does the third sentence tell you that the other two do not?
spot.answer: It is said that … and The company is thought to be … report a claim but name nobody. They use a passive: is said, is thought. According to a post I saw names the source, so you can judge it. Here the source is a post on social media, which is exactly why Mei is sceptical.

rules.title: Reporting with the passive
rule: It + is said / thought / believed / reported + that: It is said that the factory will close.
Or start with the person or thing: subject + is said / thought + to + verb.
The director is thought to be leaving. Prices are expected to rise.
An earlier event: to have + past participle: The company is said to have lost money.
Both forms report a claim and name nobody. Ask: said by whom?
rules.mistake: Not: Is said that the factory will close. Say: It is said that the factory will close.

rules.title: How headlines work
rule: Present simple for a finished event: Minister resigns = the minister has resigned.
A past participle alone is a passive: Jobs cut = jobs have been cut.
to + verb is the future: Factory to close = the factory is going to close.
Small words disappear: a, the, is, are, has, have.
A headline is the strongest version of the story. Read the article too.
rules.mistake: Jobs cut does not mean the jobs cut something. It means jobs have been cut.

practice.q: ___ said that the new bridge will cost twice as much as planned.
practice.why: The reporting passive needs it: It is said that …

practice.q: The director is thought ___ the company next year.
practice.why: Subject + is thought + to + verb: is thought to be leaving.

practice.q: The company is said ___ a lot of money last year.
practice.why: For an earlier event, use to have + past participle.

practice.q: It ___ that the fire started in the kitchen.
practice.why: It + is + past participle + that: It is believed that …

practice.q: Headline: MAYOR RESIGNS. What does it mean?
options: The mayor is going to resign.
practice.why: In a headline, the present simple reports a finished event.

practice.q: Headline: FACTORY TO CLOSE. What does it mean?
options: The factory is going to close.
practice.a: The factory is going to close.
practice.why: In a headline, to + verb talks about the future.

practice.q: Headline: 200 JOBS CUT AT PORT. What does it mean?
options: 200 jobs have been cut at the port.
200 workers cut something at the port.
200 jobs will be cut next year.
practice.a: 200 jobs have been cut at the port.
practice.why: A past participle alone in a headline is a passive: have been cut.

practice.q: The driver is thought to ___ the country last week.
practice.why: An earlier event: to have + past participle.

practice.q: It is ___ that the storm will reach the coast tonight.
practice.why: It is + past participle + that: It is expected that …

practice.q: Prices are expected ___ again next month.
practice.why: Subject + is expected + to + verb: are expected to rise.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a story you heard recently, at work, in your town or in the news, that you are not sure is true. Write three sentences that report it carefully, and then a headline of five words or fewer.
yourTurn.model: It is said that the council is going to close the swimming pool on Park Road. The building is thought to need repairs that would cost over a million pounds. Nobody from the council has confirmed it yet. Headline: Park Road pool to close?

text.title: One story, three outlets
text.body:
PRACTICE TEXT: the company, the town and all three outlets are invented.

THE MILLBROOK EXAMINER · local newspaper, Tuesday
NORLAND FOODS REVIEWS FUTURE OF MILLBROOK SITE
Norland Foods has confirmed that it is reviewing the future of its factory in Millbrook, which employs 420 people. In a press release published on Monday evening, the company said that 'no final decision has been made' and that staff would be 'kept fully informed'.
A spokesperson for the company declined to comment on reports that 300 jobs are at risk. The Examiner has not been able to verify this figure, and no independent source has confirmed it. The local union said it had asked for an urgent meeting. We check every figure for accuracy before we publish it.
---
NEWSWIRE 24 · news website, Tuesday
UP TO 300 JOBS 'AT RISK' AT NORLAND FOODS
Up to 300 jobs are reportedly at risk at Norland Foods' Millbrook factory, according to the Central Press Agency. The agency quoted an anonymous source at the company, who said that managers had been told to 'prepare for the worst'. It is thought that production could move to the company's larger site in Wales. Norland Foods did not respond to a request for comment.
---
THE DAILY BUZZ · entertainment and gossip site, Tuesday
EXCLUSIVE: FACTORY SHUTS, 300 JOBS AXED
In an exclusive story, the Buzz can reveal that the Millbrook factory will shut its doors for good before Christmas, with 300 workers losing their jobs. 'Everyone is in shock,' one worker told us. Bosses are said to have known about the plan for months. Share this story if you think it's a scandal!

gist.q: What do all three outlets report?
gist.a: The future of the Millbrook factory is in question.
gist.why: All three report a possible change at the factory; only the Buzz says it will definitely shut.

gist.q: Which outlet claims the most, with the least support?
gist.why: It says the factory will shut, but it quotes only one unnamed worker.

detail.q: What did Norland Foods itself say?
detail.a: No final decision has been made.
wrong: The factory will close before Christmas.
detail.why: Its press release said that no final decision had been made.

detail.q: Where does Newswire 24's figure of 300 jobs come from?
detail.a: an agency, which quoted an anonymous source
detail.why: It reports the figure according to the Central Press Agency, which quoted an anonymous source.

detail.q: Norland Foods did not respond to a request for comment. What does this tell you?
detail.a: Newswire asked the company, and the company said nothing.
detail.why: It means the outlet asked for a comment and got no reply.

detail.q: Which outlet is most careful about the figure of 300 jobs?
detail.a: the Examiner, which says it could not verify it
wrong: the Buzz, which calls its story exclusive
Newswire, which repeats what the agency said
detail.why: The Examiner says it has not been able to verify the figure.

items.meaning: An organisation that publishes or broadcasts news, such as a newspaper, a website or a TV channel.
items.example: The story appeared in three outlets on the same morning.

items.meaning: In the news: a company that collects news and sells it to newspapers, websites and TV channels.
items.example: Most papers took the story from the same agency.

items.meaning: An official statement that an organisation gives to journalists.
items.example: The council announced the plan in a press release.

items.meaning: A person whose job is to speak to journalists and the public for an organisation.
items.example: A spokesperson for the hospital said the ward would reopen on Monday.

items.meaning: With a name that is not known or not given.
items.example: The information came from an anonymous caller.

items.meaning: Not connected with, or controlled by, the people or organisation involved.
items.example: The figures were checked by an independent expert.

items.meaning: Reported by only one outlet, which says it has the story first.
items.example: The paper ran an exclusive interview with the manager.

items.meaning: According to what people say, although it has not been checked or proved.
items.example: The singer is reportedly planning a new tour.

items.meaning: To print something, or put it online, so that the public can read it.
items.example: The report will be published on Friday.

items.meaning: To check that something is true or correct.
items.example: We could not verify the caller's name.

items.meaning: The quality of being correct and exact, with no mistakes.
items.example: Check the dates for accuracy before you send the report.

model.title: Who claims what
model.body:
Norland Foods: what we know so far
Norland Foods has confirmed that it is reviewing the future of its Millbrook factory. In a press release, the company said that no final decision had been made. According to the Central Press Agency, up to 300 jobs are at risk, but this figure comes from one anonymous source and has not been verified. The Daily Buzz claims that the factory will close before Christmas. However, it quotes only one unnamed worker, and no other outlet gives a date. It is thought that production could move to Wales, but the company has not commented. In short, a change seems likely, but the details have not been confirmed.

write.task: Choose a news story you know, or invent one. Write a short report of 100–150 words that says who claims what. Name each source, say what it claims, and say what has not been checked yet. Use at least one reporting passive.
checklist: I named each source: a spokesperson, an agency, an anonymous source …
I used a reporting passive: It is said that … or … is thought to …
I said what has not been checked or verified.
I ended with one sentence about what we know so far.

card.title: Present a news story
card.situation: Choose a news story from the last few weeks: from your country, your town, your work or your field. It can be serious or light. You will present it in the live class, and the others will ask you about it.
card.goal: Tell the story in about two minutes, say where it came from, and say how far you trust it, and why. Then answer questions.

phrases: The story I've chosen is about …
It is said that … / … is thought to …
The source is …, so I'd say it's fairly trustworthy.
I'd take it with a pinch of salt until …
prepare.notes: Write short notes: what happened, who reported it, who the source is, whether anyone has checked it, and who might gain from the story. Finish with one sentence: how far you trust it, and what would change your mind.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, each learner presents a story for about two minutes. The others ask questions: Who is the source? Has anyone else reported it? Then the group decides together: trust it, doubt it, or wait and see.
doIt.wehel: You are a journalist and my colleague. I will tell you about a news story and say how far I trust it. Ask me questions, one at a time: who the source is, whether it has been checked, and what other outlets say. After five questions, tell me if my judgement sounds reasonable, and correct any mistakes I make with It is said that or is thought to.

model.title: A story about rents
lines: Omar
The story I've chosen is about rents in our city. Last week, a headline said: Rents rise by a third.
Ana
A third? That sounds very high. Where did you see it?
Omar
It went viral on social media, but it was first published by a property website.
Ana
And who was the source?
Omar
According to the website, the figure came from its own adverts. It is said that the average rent went up from nine hundred to twelve hundred pounds a month.
Ana
Did anyone else check it?
Omar
That's the problem. No independent source has verified it. And the website makes its money from landlords, so it may not be neutral.
Ana
So how far do you trust it?
Omar
I think rents are rising. My own rent went up last year. But I'd take the figure of a third with a pinch of salt. Adverts show the asking price, not what people actually pay.
Ana
What would change your mind?
Omar
Official figures, or a report from an independent organisation. If they said the same, I'd believe it.
compare: Did you say clearly what the story was?
Did you name the source and say how it knows?
Did you say how far you trust the story, with a reason?
Did you say what would change your mind?

canDo: I can discuss a news story and say where I heard it.
I can use reporting passives like It is said that and is thought to.
I can read a headline and say what it does and does not claim.
I can compare reports of one story and write who claims what.
I can present a news story and say how far I trust it, and why.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first paragraph. Who is telling this story, and how do they know? Do you trust them yet?
reading.talk: Which parts of the text are facts, and which are claims? Who is the source for each one? Write three or four sentences with According to … or It is said that …, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: ___ is said that the manager has resigned.
quiz.why: The reporting passive starts with It: It is said that …

quiz.q: The singer is thought ___ married last year.
quiz.why: For an earlier event, use to have + past participle.

quiz.q: Headline: CAR BAN TO START IN MAY. What does it mean?
options: A car ban will start in May.
A car ban started in May.
Cars started a ban in May.
quiz.a: A car ban will start in May.
quiz.why: In a headline, to + verb talks about the future.

quiz.q: A story that people pass on, which may not be true, is a ___ .
quiz.why: A rumour may or may not be true.

quiz.q: The company did not respond to a request for comment. What does this mean?
options: They were asked and said nothing.
quiz.a: They were asked and said nothing.
quiz.why: Did not respond means there was no reply at all.

quiz.q: I'm ___ about stories with no named source.
quiz.why: Sceptical means you doubt whether something is true.

quiz.q: Which source is usually the most trustworthy?
options: a named spokesperson, speaking on the record
an anonymous post on social media
a headline on a gossip site
quiz.a: a named spokesperson, speaking on the record
quiz.why: A named person on the record can be checked.

quiz.q: Whether we go ___ on the weather.
quiz.why: Whether we go is one thing, so depends on.

quiz.q: He ___ taking the money, but the camera showed that he had.
quiz.why: To deny something is to say you did not do it.

quiz.q: If I ___ the forecast, I would have taken an umbrella.
quiz.why: The if half of a third conditional: had + past participle.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Carlos and Mei's conversation in pairs, then a rumour chain: one learner reads out a made-up headline, the next passes it on with Apparently … or According to …, and the group checks how the story changed.
Day 2: the task. Each learner presents a news story in about two minutes and says how far they trust it. The others ask about the source, then the group decides: trust it, doubt it, or wait and see.
Day 3: talk about the book: who is the source for each claim in it? Then two or three learners read their who-claims-what reports aloud, and the group checks that every claim has a source.
